extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, political science scholars, and researchers studying peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of why invited scholars accept, decline, or fail to complete manuscript review requests for an academic journal (APSR), and recommendations for editorial practices to manage reviewer workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'reviewer fatigue'
rubrics_metrics.description: We define 'reviewer fatigue' as statements indicating scholars decline because they have other reviews to complete and/or cannot take on an additional review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note this is a somewhat narrow definition; some respondents who say they are 'too busy' may reflect reviewer fatigue, so combining 'too many invitations' with 'too busy' yields a broader (but possibly overstated) measure of fatigue. In the study, reviewer fatigue accounts for 14.1% of declines (19.7% of those who provided a reason); combined 'too many invitations' + 'too busy' accounts for 38.9% of declines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response rate to review invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of invited reviewers who reply (either accept or decline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the APSR 2013 data 82.8% of requests elicited a response; 17.2% did not respond. Non-responsiveness can result from outdated e-mail addresses or spam filters as well as choice not to reply, so non-response is not purely a behavioral refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rate of review requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of invitations accepted (measured either per request or per responding request).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using all requests as denominator, 60% were accepted. Using only requests that got a response, 72.5% were accepted (27.5% declined). Women and men accept in similar proportions; differences not statistically significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion rate after acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of accepted review assignments that are actually completed and submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the data, 77.6% of accepted assignments were completed. Noncompletion arises from two main types: (1) editors 'unassign' reviewers when a decision can be made after other reviews, and (2) reviewers who do not complete despite reminders. Editors may invite additional reviewers when necessary, lengthening decision time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of requests per individual
rubrics_metrics.description: How many review invitations individual scholars receive (e.g., one, two, three or more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 73.3% of scholars received only one request, 20.9% received two, and 5.8% received three or more. Of those with multiple requests, 14.1% were for resubmissions. Editorial board members were more likely to receive multiple requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of subfield on acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance propensity varies by the manuscript's subfield classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance is higher in subfields traditionally associated with the journal (e.g., American politics and closely affiliated areas) and lower in other subfields. The authors note significant statistical differences across subfields (table 3; Chi-square significant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of methodology on acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance propensity varies by the manuscript's methodological classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater variability in acceptance exists across methodological classifications than across subfields. Papers using methods traditionally associated with the journal (e.g., quantitative work for APSR) had higher acceptance rates. Methodology composition of submissions (e.g., two-thirds quantitative) may shape reviewer expectations and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization of self-reported reasons for declining
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic categories used to code why scholars decline review invitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categories include: provided no reason (28.3% of declines), 'too busy' (24.8% of declines), 'too many invitations' / reviewer fatigue (14.1%), previously reviewed for another journal, conflict of interest, travel commitments (professional or leisure combined), administrative duties, personal/family illness or leave, journal editors declining (often citing editorial workload), and 'other' (e.g., leaving academia, retiring, low interest based on abstract). The authors note gendered differences across these categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy re: suggesting alternative reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether declining reviewers suggest alternative reviewers and how this correlates with giving a reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who provided a reason were more likely to suggest one or more alternative reviewers. Almost 60% of decliners did not suggest alternatives. The authors state that providing alternative reviewer names is 'useful and welcome.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender distribution and differences in reviewer behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: How requests, acceptances, completions, and reasons for declining differ by gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women received 30.6% of requests (roughly proportional to their presence in the field). Women and men accept and complete at similar rates. However, women were somewhat more likely to cite being 'too busy', having too many requests, or being on leave; men were somewhat more likely to cite insufficient expertise, administrative duties, being journal editors, or having previously read the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial strategies to broaden and improve reviewer recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices editors can use to reduce repeated requests to the same scholars and to improve responsiveness and completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations from the authors include: systematically include first-time reviewers and new PhDs and research-active scholars from a broader range of institutions; use web-based search strategies (dissertation databases, recent conference programs, Google Scholar) to broaden the reviewer pool; send personal e-mails (not only automated reminders) to late reviewers to improve responsiveness. These strategies require time but can broaden participation and improve efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and generalizability of single-journal, single-year data
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveats about applying these findings beyond the APSR 2013 dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study is based on one journal and one year; response, acceptance, and completion rates may vary across journals, years, and by prestige or field. The authors emphasize that some behaviors (e.g., prioritizing prestigious journals) are empirical questions needing broader study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives and prosocial framing of reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations on the role of incentives and prosocial behavior in review completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing related work, the authors note reviewing is a prosocial behavior and that incentives can facilitate timely completion of reviews (Chetty et al. 2014). While this study did not test incentives directly, it affirms the value of studying peer review empirically and suggests incentives may be a lever to improve performance.
